title: Comparative Impact of ChatGPT and Conventional Search Tools on Clinical Reasoning Performance: A Randomized Crossover Study in Preclinical Medical Students
venue: Advances in Medical Education and Practice
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language model–based AI support, specifically ChatGPT, improves clinical reasoning performance in medical education compared with conventional information-seeking tools such as Google or PubMed. The authors focus on preclinical learners because clinical reasoning is a core medical competency, but there is limited controlled evidence on how generative AI affects reasoning-oriented learning rather than factual recall.

The study used a randomized crossover design during a musculoskeletal system course. Forty-six second-year medical students at Kasetsart University in Thailand completed a baseline clinical reasoning pre-test, then used either ChatGPT or conventional search tools to analyze standardized clinical cases. After a post-test, students had a 60-minute washout period and crossed over to the alternate modality, followed by another post-test. Clinical reasoning was scored with an eight-point rubric covering domains such as problem representation, differential diagnosis, investigations, and management planning. Secondary data included self-perceived learning, confidence, and qualitative feedback.

Scores improved significantly from pre-test to post-test 1 and again after crossover, with a large cumulative effect size from baseline to the final post-test. The results did not show that improvement was attributable to one tool alone; rather, both ChatGPT and conventional search supported learning in different ways. Students reported that ChatGPT helped rapidly organize differential diagnoses and management plans, while conventional search promoted comparison across multiple information sources and more deliberate synthesis.

The authors conclude that AI-assisted tools and conventional search strategies can play complementary roles in structured active-learning environments. They recommend balanced integration of large language models into undergraduate medical education, with faculty oversight and explicit emphasis on verifying AI-generated information to reduce risks from hallucinations or inaccurate outputs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: ChatGPT is an OpenAI large language model chatbot that generates conversational, context-sensitive responses and can synthesize information for educational use.
identified_tools.use_case: Second-year medical students used ChatGPT during a 20-minute structured case-based search activity to analyze standardized musculoskeletal clinical cases using self-directed prompting, then completed rubric-scored clinical reasoning post-tests.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized crossover study with 46 second-year medical students, mean clinical reasoning rubric scores increased from 3.96 (SD 1.65) at pre-test to 4.96 (SD 1.71) after the first intervention and 5.70 (SD 1.50) after crossover. Paired comparisons were statistically significant for pre-test to post-test 1 (t(45)=-3.79, p<0.05), post-test 1 to post-test 2 (t(45)=-2.96, p<0.05), and pre-test to post-test 2 (t(45)=-6.57, p<0.05), with a large cumulative effect size (Cohen’s d=0.97). The authors state that improvements occurred across both ChatGPT and conventional search modalities, without evidence that gains were attributable to a single approach.
findings.measure: Clinical reasoning performance measured using an eight-point rubric-based scale
findings.effect_size: Cohen’s d=0.56 for pre-test to post-test 1; Cohen’s d=0.44 for post-test 1 to post-test 2; Cohen’s d=0.97 for pre-test to post-test 2

findings.finding_summary: Students qualitatively reported that ChatGPT facilitated rapid organization of differential diagnoses and management plans. They also emphasized the importance of verifying AI outputs against reliable references; quantitative results for self-perceived learning or confidence were not reported.
findings.measure: Self-perceived learning, confidence, and qualitative feedback

quality_tier_rationale: This was a randomized crossover study with all 46 participants completing both phases and paired analyses reported. Credibility concerns include the single-institution preclinical sample, short-term assessment only, possible residual period/carryover effects, and limited modality-specific outcome reporting.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported cumulative improvement in clinical reasoning performance was large (Cohen’s d=0.97) and statistically significant. However, the effect was reported for the structured crossover experience involving both ChatGPT and conventional search, not as an isolated ChatGPT-only effect.
